newsitem.title: ITALY: Pirelli profits leap and div doubles.
newsitem.headline: Pirelli profits leap and div doubles.

text.p: Italy's tyre and cables group Pirelli turned out a sparkling set of 1996 results on Wednesday with annual net profits up 43 percent, the dividend doubled and the promise of more to come.

The Milan-based company added a 300 billion lire ($178 million) share buyback proposal to its above-forecast results, and analysts now expect the shares to start firmer on Thursday despite their already high rating on the Milan bourse.

"For Pirelli, 1997 is set to continue the positive trends seen in 1996 and first quarter trading has been in line with this pattern," Pirelli's chairman and chief executive Marco Tronchetti Provera told a results news conference.

The group reported consolidated net profits of 436 billion lire against 304 billion lire in 1995, while the net line after minorities, largely minority shareholders in Pirelli's Tyre business, rose 51 percent to 387 billion lire from 257 billion.

"Even allowing for the excellent 1996 results the company is probably close to fair value on its prospects for this year," said analyst Nick Potter at brokers Credito Italiano, who sees Pirelli as one of Italy's top performing companies due to its efficiencies and its truly global spread.

The company doubled the dividend on its ordinary shares for 1996 to 100 lire a share from 50 lire in 1995, which in itself was the first dividend Pirelli has paid since 1990. The dividend on its savings shares rose to 120 lire from 70 lire a share.
It also proposed the purchase of its own shares up to a maximum of 300 billion lire to be made within the next 18 months through the use of its retained earnings.

The strength of the Italian currency through 1996 sliced into the translation of the group's sales into lire and 1996 turnover fell six percent to 10.24 trillion lire, although actual sales volumes rose 3.3 percent for the year.

This 9.3 percent difference between the sales fall and volume growth was accounted for by a reduction of 4.7 percent due to exchange rates, 2.9 percent for price falls and 1.7 percent in the deterioration of the product mix.
Analysts said that despite the strength of the lira, profits managed to push strongly ahead due to good cost control and as the radical restructuring started in 1991 began to bear fruit.

Pirelli produced a string of losses between 1991 and 1993 as the group was hit by economic recession, a depressed automobile market and the hefty cost of restructuring, but bounced back to profits in 1994 and the figures have been climbing ever since.
Operating profits rose 6.9 percent to 680 billion lire, while net debt declined leading to lower interest charges, and the group's tax charge was also lower in 1996.
Credito's Potter is now looking for 1997 net profit after minorities of 460 billion and a dividend of 120 lire a share.
Pirelli's business is almost equally split between cables and tyres, with cables seeing sales fall 7.4 percent largely due to the lira's strength while net income rose 27.6 percent.

The tyres side showed sales down 4.6 percent but net income up 63 percent led by strong growth in South America, particularly Brazil, and positive performances in Turkey and Asia. Europe showed a stable trend with good performances from Britain and Germany, while north America was positive.

In January this year, Pirelli launched a bid for the shares it did not own in its Amsterdam-listed Pirelli Tyre Holding NV company, which includes all its world-wide tyre interests, and has since raised its stake to 99.53 percent. ($1=1,684 lire)
